evidence.source: Shuowen5, 高 entry (reproduces Shuowen and Duan Yucai annotation)
evidence.text: The entry gives the received Shuowen account: 高 means ‘崇’ and its form depicts a tall 臺觀 (raised building/viewing tower); Shuowen analyzes it with 冂 and 口 and compares the formation with 倉 and 舍. Duan Yucai’s note further glosses the comparison in terms of enclosing/building forms. This is an early lexicographic analysis, not independent proof of every component’s original referent.

evidence.text: The database indexes 高 examples under oracle-bone script, bronze inscriptions, Chu bamboo/silk, and small seal/Shuowen. It identifies a Western Zhou bronze vessel inscription and a mid-Warring-States bronze inscription among its examples. The page’s text labels establish categories and artifact captions; I did not visually inspect the glyph images, so I do not claim specific stroke-by-stroke changes from them.

evidence.source: Education Ministry of Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry records 高 as the standard form and lists variants including 髙. It repeats the Shuowen tower account and notes a traditional analysis with 冂 and 口. Its modern pronunciation is Mandarin gāo. Its cited literary examples distinguish senses including vertical height (《禮記·曲禮上》), a high ridge (《詩經·周南·卷耳》, ‘陟彼高岡’), excellence, esteem, high price, old age, and a high or forceful voice. The page does not date the initial emergence of these extensions; its gloss sequence is not a chronology.
evidence.title: [A04667] 高 - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: Chinese Etymology, Education University of Hong Kong resource
evidence.text: The entry describes oracle-bone, bronze, and small-seal forms as resembling a tall pavilion, with the building image used to represent ‘high’. Its text states that the standard form follows small seal. This supports the pictographic interpretation, though the accessible entry does not document detailed dated forms or competing readings.

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 高 entry (pronunciation tables citing Baxter–Sagart and Zhengzhang systems)
evidence.text: Modern Beijing Mandarin is gāo; Cantonese is gou1. The entry gives Middle Chinese kaw (Baxter reconstruction; Guangyun fanqie 古勞切, level tone) and Old Chinese *Cə.[k]ˤaw in Baxter–Sagart 1.1 (2014), compared with Zhengzhang’s *kaːw (2003). Both systems represent the character’s word, not a separate phonetic component: 高 is analyzed as pictographic, so no sound component is proposed here. The entry glosses high/tall and records extensions such as above-average level, high place, loud voice, and honorific use, but these are not dated semantic stages.

evidence.text: The search-result description for 京 states that its oracle-bone and bronze forms depict a tall structure and describes a roof, central tower, and lower wall, with the central portion simplified in small seal. This is a close graphic parallel to the dossier’s comparison with 京, but resemblance does not demonstrate that 京 is a component, ancestor, or source of 高.
evidence.title: 漢字「京」：字形演變

evidence.text: The entry reports a possible relationship between the Chinese words 高 and 喬, while explicitly leaving the derivational relationship unresolved. This is a lexical comparison, not a graphic component analysis: no basis was found here to classify 喬 as a component of 高 or to assert a definite cognate relation.

gaps: No dated primary oracle-bone or bronze inscription occurrence was verified in the inspected pages; the database lists inscription corpora and artifacts, but its relevant glyph images were not visually inspected here.

The exact earliest attested lexical sense and the dates/paths of extensions such as ‘excellent’, ‘esteemed’, ‘expensive’, ‘old’, and ‘loud’ remain unresolved. The official dictionary supplies citations but not a semantic chronology.

Shuowen’s segmentation into 冂 and 口 is recorded as a historical analysis. The available sources do not independently establish those parts’ separate original semantic contributions or prove the analysis is historically accurate.
The visual resemblance and comparison with 京 do not establish common ancestry or borrowing. No whole-graph loan claim was found or advanced.

The dossier’s Proto-Sino-Tibetan ‘head’ proposal and proposed relation to 喬/H 浩 were not independently substantiated by inspected primary evidence; no relation is asserted. 高 has no proposed phonetic component, so component pronunciation and origin_relation classifications do not apply.

The accessible comparison source describes broad form categories and some artifact captions, but the actual images were not visually inspected; detailed graphic transitions and possible scribal corruption remain undetermined.

The pronunciation sources provide competing Old Chinese reconstructions under named systems, not direct recordings. The chronology or semantic connection between building depiction and the adjective ‘high’ is strongly suggested by the lexicographic account but not independently established through a dated earliest-use chain.
